title: A magnet falls slowly down an aluminium tube, though it won't stick to aluminium

cover.alt: A hand holds a small spherical magnet above a slotted aluminium tube standing upright on a wooden table.

body: As the magnet falls, the magnetic field passing through each part of the tube keeps changing, and a changing field drives loops of electric current, called **eddy currents**, in the metal. By Lenz's law, those currents make magnetic fields that oppose the change that created them, so they drag against the magnet's motion and it sinks slowly instead of dropping. The energy of the fall ends up as a little heat in the metal. The same contact-free drag helps stop some trains and roller coasters.

slides.alt: A hand drops a small spherical magnet into an upright slotted aluminium tube; it takes a moment to come out at the bottom. Then the magnet is dropped beside the tube and hits the table at once, and finally dropped into the tube again.
slides.caption: Dropped into a slotted aluminium tube, the magnet drifts down slowly; you can glimpse it through the slot. Dropped beside the tube, it hits the table at once.

slides.heading: Why the tube slows the magnet

steps.label: The magnet falls down the tube
The field through the metal keeps changing
Their fields oppose the fall and slow it

left.label: Beside the tube
left.text: Nothing but air in the way, so it falls freely and lands almost at once.

right.label: Down the tube
right.text: Currents induced in the metal oppose its motion, and it sinks at a slow pace.

slides.question: Why don't eddy current brakes wear out like ordinary brakes?
options: Their magnets are made of rubber
slides.explanation: The drag comes from currents induced in the moving metal, so there's no brake shoe to wear. They can't hold a vehicle still, though, so they may be paired with mechanical brakes.
